opus-5.5.text:
I think the concerns are justified because medical data is about as personal as information gets, and once it's out there, you can't take it back. If your credit card number gets leaked, you cancel the card and get a new one. If your genome or your cancer diagnosis or your mental health history gets exposed, there's no reissuing that. It follows you for the rest of your life, and in the case of genetic data, it implicates your relatives too, people who never consented to anything.

There's also a technical reality that I think people underestimate. We've talked for a long time about "de-identifying" data, stripping out names, birthdates, addresses, and treating that as sufficient. But study after study has shown that re-identification is surprisingly easy. A handful of attributes, like zip code, age, and sex, can single out a large fraction of people. With imaging data, a CT scan of the head can be used to reconstruct a face. And as datasets get linked together and machine learning gets better at finding patterns, the protection that de-identification once offered keeps eroding.

And then there's the question of harm. People worry, rightly, about discrimination, by employers, by insurers, in some cases socially. Legal protections exist, but they're patchy and they vary a lot depending on where you live. So when patients hesitate about their data being shared publicly, I don't see that as irrational or as an obstacle to science. It's a reasonable response to real risks.

That said, as a researcher, I also know how much value there is in that data. Sharing it is how we build better diagnostic models, how we find treatments for rare diseases, how we make sure AI tools work for diverse populations. So for me the answer isn't "never share." It's that we have to take those concerns seriously and build approaches, things like federated learning, privacy-preserving computation, strong governance, that let us get the scientific benefit without asking patients to shoulder all the risk.

r001.rationale: The response mentions possible discrimination by insurers, but it does not state that identification from accidentally released medical data can lead to denial of insurance in many parts of the world.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the concerns are justified because medical data is probably the most personal information any of us has. It's not like a credit card number that you can cancel and replace. Your genome, your diagnoses, your imaging scans, those are permanent, and they don't just describe you, they describe your family too.

And the thing people underestimate is how hard it is to truly anonymize this data. We say "de-identified," we strip the name and the date of birth, but a CT scan still contains the shape of someone's face. A rare diagnosis combined with a zip code and an approximate age can narrow things down to a handful of people. There's been research showing that with a few data points, re-identification is surprisingly feasible. So when a patient hears "we've removed the identifiers," I understand the skepticism, because the guarantee is weaker than it sounds.

Then there's the question of what happens downstream. Once data is public, you can't call it back. It could be used by insurers, by employers, by someone building a product the patient never consented to. Consent was given in one context, usually a clinical one, and it gets stretched into contexts nobody anticipated.

And I say this as someone whose work absolutely depends on access to medical data. I want more data sharing, not less, because that's how we build models that actually help patients. But if we dismiss these concerns, we lose trust, and when you lose trust, people stop participating altogether. So I'd rather we take the concerns seriously, build the governance, the controlled access, the federated approaches, and earn the right to use this data responsibly.

r001.rationale: The response says released data could be used by insurers, but does not state that re-identification can lead to someone being denied insurance or that this occurs in many parts of the world.

astra-6.text: I think those concerns are justified because medical data is deeply personal. It can reveal things about you that you haven’t shared even with people close to you. And removing someone’s name doesn’t necessarily mean they can’t be identified, especially when that data is combined with other information. Once it’s public, you lose control over who uses it and for what purpose. There’s tremendous potential for research, but we have to take patients’ privacy and trust seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says medical data can enable re-identification, but does not state that this can lead to denial of insurance in many parts of the world.
